French presidential hopeful Teddy Riner says Ukraine is ‘not our war’
articles.summary: The Olympic gold medalist’s remarks on Russia’s ongoing full-scale invasion provoked a backlash
articles.body: The Olympic gold medalist’s remarks on Russia’s ongoing full-scale invasion provoked a backlash. PARIS — Teddy Riner, the legendary judoka running for president in France, sparked controversy on Wednesday after declaring that Ukraine was not his country's conflict. "I don't understand why we're sending troops to Ukraine when it's not our war," the five-time Olympic gold medalist told reporters . Riner was referring to the deployment of French troops in Ukraine, which was criticized by opposition parties for having been decided without parliamentary approval. Deputy Defense Minister Alice Rufo said the troops are "dedicated to training and equipment maintenance." "If I become president tomorrow, I would like to be the kind of person who brings people together, who smiles and shakes hands to put an end to this war," Riner added about Russia's war in Ukraine. Russian leader Vladimir Putin also practices judo and was honorary president of the International Judo Federation before launching the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The 37-year-old Riner has unveiled few policy proposals and had not yet weighed in on foreign affairs since announcing his candidacy earlier this month . The two leading candidates for next April's election in France — far-right chief Marine Le Pen and far-left veteran Jean-Luc Mélenchon — have both been critical of current President Emmanuel Macron's Ukraine policy. Macron's government has sent funds and weapons to Ukraine and co-led the coalition of the willing, a group of Kyiv's most significant allies and supporters. Riner, however, had been more closely associated with the pro-Macron camp based on early campaign statements, making his Ukraine comments more surprising. Early surveys have shown him polling at about 4%, drawing mostly from voters who opted for Macron in the last presidential election. Center-right MEP Nathalie Loiseau, who handles foreign affairs policy for presidential candidate Edouard Philippe, seized on Riner's remarks to attack the election rival. "Teddy Riner's world would be so simple: you don't get involved in anything, you shake hands with everyone, and there's peace and love all over the world," she wrote on X . Riner was speaking from the French mayors' congress currently taking place in Paris, where he was seeking out endorsements needed to run for president. He still has a long way to go before actually getting onto the ballot: Riner said he had obtained more than 100 signatures from local officials in support his candidacy — far from the 500 needed to confirm his candidacy under French law.

articles.title: Trump, Rutte press Russia to not 'expand war'
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump and NATO chief Mark Rutte called on Russia not to "expand the war" in Ukraine
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump and NATO chief Mark Rutte called on Russia not to "expand the war" in Ukraine.

Rutte traveled to Florida for the meeting with Trump.

"We also discussed the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war, and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the war as rapidly as possible," they said in a joint statement sent by the White House.

articles.title: US senator blames Trump’s ‘illegal war’ on Iran for rising Thanksgiving costs
articles.body:
US Senator Chris Van Hollen has blamed President Donald Trump’s war on Iran and tariffs for rising food prices, saying American families are facing higher costs as they prepare to celebrate Thanksgiving.

In a Thanksgiving video posted to social media, Van Hollen said many Americans were experiencing “sticker shock”, with prices going “up and up and up”.

Citing the American Farm Bureau Federation, he said the average cost of Thanksgiving dinner had risen 6 percent compared with last year, while turkey prices had increased 10 percent.

“And we know why this is happening,” Van Hollen said.

“It’s because of Trump’s illegal war in Iran that are driving up all of our prices. It’s because of his tariff wars that are driving them up even further.”

The senator accused Trump and his wealthy allies of being insulated from the economic pressures facing everyday Americans.

He also called for political action following the recent US elections, saying, “Now it’s time for us all to deliver.”

articles.title: Woman killed, seven injured in Houthi shelling in Yemen’s Taiz
articles.summary: A woman has been killed and seven other civilians
articles.body:
A woman has been killed and seven other civilians, including a child, have been injured in Houthi shelling of villages southeast of Yemen’s Taiz city, according to the government-run Saba news agency.

Citing a local source, Saba reported that the shelling targeted villages in the Sabir al-Mawadim and al-Misrakh districts of Jabal Sabir.

The injured were taken to hospital for treatment, while several homes were also damaged in the attacks, the agency said.

Kim Jong Un tours nuclear material sites, urges wider use of tactical nuclear weapons
articles.summary: The visit took place on Wednesday, but the state news agency KCNA did not provide the location of the sites
articles.body: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un toured factories that make nuclear material, along with a research institute, and pressed for the wider use of tactical nuclear weapons, state media reported on Thursday. The visit took place on Wednesday, but the state news agency KCNA did not provide the location of the sites. Photos showed Kim walking between rows of what appeared to be centrifuges for enriching uranium. Analysts also spotted small, standardized tactical warheads such as the Hwasan-31. Kim said North Korea's production capacity for nuclear material is being steadily expanded. He said tactical weapons should be used in different areas and for different missions, citing the danger from a hostile state on his border, referring to neighbor South Korea . He also accused the United States of encouraging its allies to seek nuclear-powered submarines and to share nuclear weapons. "Our possession of nuclear weapons is an absolutely irreversible choice as long as malicious forces exist that use nuclear weapons as a means of achieving hegemony," Kim said, adding that he would treat any attempt to deny North Korea's nuclear status, which was written into its constitution in 2023, as a declaration of war. Kim said Pyongyang would not seek approval from other countries. Lim Eul-chul, a professor at South Korea's Kyungnam University, said the visit signals Kim's desire to change the circumstances of any future talks on North Korea's weapons programs. "This is not so much North Korea permanently closing the door to dialogue with the United States as a strategy of raising the bar: 'denuclearisation talks' are over, and if talks open in future, it will deal only on a 'nuclear state versus nuclear state' basis," he told Reuters news agency. South Korean news agency Yonhap said this was Kim's fourth visit to a nuclear facility since September 2024. It came about a week after US President Donald Trump visited China for the APEC summit, where Kim did not publicly respond to an offer to meet. articles.title: Russia launches fresh ballistic missile attack on Kyiv
articles.summary: Russia launched more ballistic missiles at the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, late on Wednesday
articles.body:
Russia launched more ballistic missiles at the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, late on Wednesday.

Explosions were heard in the city, and a building in an industrial area was hit, Mayor Vitali Klitschko wrote on Telegram. He said residents should remain in shelters.

The Ukrainian air force confirmed the Russian attack. Telegram channels linked to the military reported that up to eight missiles had been fired from Russia's Bryansk region near the Ukrainian border. The missiles reportedly targeted districts of Kyiv east of the Dnipro River.

The full extent of the damage was not immediately clear.

Russia has stepped up attacks on infrastructure in Kyiv and other major Ukrainian cities in recent months, seeking to disrupt electricity, heating and water supplies.

Ukraine has struggled to defend itself against ballistic missiles amid shortages of interceptor missiles for its US-made Patriot air defense systems.

articles.title: US envoy warns against escalation of war in Ukraine
articles.body:
In an interview with the German MD Meets Podcast, US envoy Jared Kushner warned against a downward spiral in the conflict in Ukraine, which he described as "a proxy war where Europe is funding and arming Ukraine against Russia."

Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law and chosen intermediary in negotiations with Russia's Vladimir Putin, also warned that "it won't take a lot of miscalculation for this thing to escalate massively."

After several failed rounds of talks involving his fellow envoy, Steve Witkoff, Kushner admitted that the issue of territoriy in eastern Ukraine remained a sticking point.

"What Steve and I have deciphered from having many, many hours with President Putin and from the Russian team, is that you know the territorial issue is right now a little bit of a deadlock," he said.

However, Kushner also appeared to accuse the Europeans of hypocrisy for supporting Ukraine while continuing to spend vast sums of money on Russian energy.

articles.title: Berlin trial of woman suspected of spying for Russia set to start
articles.summary: A German-Ukrainian woman accused of spying for Russia goes on trial in Berlin on Thursday
articles.body:
A German-Ukrainian woman accused of spying for Russia goes on trial in Berlin on Thursday.

She is charged with providing an employee and secret agent at the Russian Embassy in Berlin with sensitive information.

The alleged spy is accused of tipping the man off about high intelligence-value events over a period of years and helping him to secure entry.

The dpa news agency reports that the Russian agent in question was the country's deputy military attache, who has since been expelled from Germany.

The woman had long been known as a pro-Russian networker in the Berlin area, having lived in the country for several decades.

The lawsuit against her from the federal prosecutor's office based in Karslruhe also alleges that she tried to "win over individuals from the Federal Defense Ministry and the weapons industry for her purposes."

She is accused of acting out of personal conviction, rather than, say, fear or blackmail. She was arrested in January this year.

The woman is accused of making contact with the Russian espionage asset as of October 2023 at the latest. Her most pressing task was to seek out information pertaining to Germany defense policy and the weapons industry, particularly in light of and where relevant to Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

articles.title: Russian sources say Europeans must take up Putin's offer for Moscow talks
articles.body:
Numerous sources inside Russian foreign policy circles on Wednesday underscored the Kremlin's desire for European diplomats to travel to Moscow and explain their intentions before they be allowed to participate in any Russia-Ukraine peace negotiations.

Russian President Vladimir Putin originally extended the invitation last month. On Wednesday, Foreign Policy Advisor Yury Ushakov said the invitation stands but that no Europeans have so far agreed to embark on the diplomatic sojourn.

Russia's Ambassador to Germany Sergei Nechayev on Wednesday told France's AFP news agency that reaction to Putin's invitation has been "restrained."

Nechayev claimed that Moscow remains, "ready to continue the dialogue and carry on with negotiations."

He also repeated the Kremlin claim that it is Europe that is the impediment to stopping the war, and that Russia — which launched and continues to execute its unprovoked years-long war of aggression in Ukraine — is the only party truly interested in peace.

Nechayev said the Kremlin doesn't see the same "honesty" from the Europeans that it does from US President Donald Trump's team — made up of his son-in-law Jared Kushner and his friend Steve Witkoff — and wants to "know precisely what their intentions are."

Russia has been accused of foot dragging as a way to prolong attacks on Ukraine. On Wednesday, Nechayev continued in that vein, saying: "Our request to Europe is this: Decide what it is you want, determine whom you will appoint as negotiators, and, most importantly, clarify what you aim to achieve."

articles.title: India condemns attack on Riyadh Tower which injured two Indians
articles.summary: India's foreign Ministry on Wednesday "strongly condemned" the Houthi attack on one of the towers of the financial district in Riyadh
articles.body:
India's foreign Ministry on Wednesday "strongly condemned" the Houthi attack on one of the towers of the financial district in Riyadh, which injured at least 11 people including two Indians.

"These attacks seriously endanger civilian lives, violate the sovereignty of Saudi Arabia, and undermine regional security and stability. We call for immediate cessation of such attacks," the ministry said in a statement.

"We also reiterate our firm solidarity with the people and government of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and reaffirm our unwavering support to the Kingdom in safeguarding its sovereignty, territorial integrity, and the security and safety of its citizens and residents," the statement said, expressing hope that "peace and normalcy" return to the region at the earliest.

On Tuesday, India's mission in Saudi Arabia had acknowledged that two of the 11 people injured in the attack were Indians and that all assistance would be provided to them and their families.

Riyadh's tallest skyscraper was truck for a second time in days on Tuesday, in what the Saudi coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis called was a "terrorist attack."

The building was reportedly the 80-storey Public Investment Fund Tower which houses the kingdom's sovereign wealth fund and dominates the city's financial district.

On Wednesday, a day after the attack, a Houthi military spokesperson claimed the attack on the building.

articles.body:
Yemen’s Houthi group has struck the port of Jizan on Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea coast as fighting intensifies near the Yemeni city of Taiz.

A Saudi-led military coalition said a Houthi attack on Jizan caused only minor damage and no civilian casualties on Wednesday, adding that “efforts are underway to determine the type of projectile” used.

articles.title: IRGC official praises Basij role in Iran’s ‘third imposed war’
articles.body:
Hossein Maroufi, deputy for cultural affairs in the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), has praised the role of the Basij paramilitary force in Iran’s wars, describing its members as symbols of national sacrifice.

According to the Fars news agency, Maroufi said the Basij had demonstrated the Iranian people’s willingness to sacrifice themselves during what he called the country’s “third imposed war”.

He said Iranians had spent nearly 270 days confronting what he described as the world’s “devils and arrogant powers”, praising the Basij’s role in the conflict.

The Basij, a volunteer paramilitary force affiliated with the IRGC, played a domestic security role during the US-Israeli war, including conducting patrols and staffing checkpoints.

Iranian authorities also expanded recruitment and military training through a mobilisation campaign, aimed at preparing volunteers to support the country’s defence and security operations.

articles.title: Yemeni armed forces report clashes with Houthis in Marib and al-Jawf
articles.body:
Yemen’s armed forces have engaged in fierce clashes with Houthi fighters across fronts in northern Marib and southeastern al-Jawf, according to a statement posted on X by the Yemeni Armed Forces Media Centre.

On the northern front in Marib, fighting took place in the Mahzam Mas area of the Majzar district, roughly 80km from the capital, Sanaa, the statement said.

Artillery units targeted Houthi positions, heavy weapons emplacements and engineering equipment in the al-Kassara sector, as well as gatherings in the Hailan sector northwest of Marib, destroying combat vehicles and killing or wounding fighters.

Rocket launchers also struck Houthi gatherings and supply lines in Mahzam Mas, burning vehicles and destroying fortifications, the military said.

On the southeastern al-Hazm front in al-Jawf province, forces confronted Houthi attacks while artillery shelled gatherings in al-Aqsha and the village of Umm al-Jana, along with positions inside the al-Labinat camp in the al-Jadafer sector, inflicting casualties and equipment losses, it added.

“Burchuladze and other political prisoners must be released” – European Parliament draft resolution
articles.summary: Debates on a draft resolution concerning Georgia will be held in the European Parliament on November 25
articles.body: Debates on a draft resolution concerning Georgia will be held in the European Parliament on November 25. The resolution concerns the case of Paata Burchuladze and political prisoners under the Georgian Dream government. The vote is scheduled for November 26. The document calls for the immediate and unconditional release of all political prisoners and unlawfully detained individuals, regardless of their political affiliation. Those named in the resolution include Paata Burchuladze, Irakli Nadiradze, and Paata Manjgaladze. The authors of a draft resolution in the European Parliament describe the charges against Paata Burchuladze as politically motivated. The 71-year-old opera singer and civil activist was sentenced to seven years in prison in May 2026. The so-called “peaceful overthrow” case is linked to a protest held in Tbilisi on October 4, 2025. Burchuladze denies the charges. The resolution’s authors question the fairness of the trial and the proportionality of the sentence. They also raise concerns about Burchuladze’s prolonged isolation, strict restrictions on contact with the outside world and inadequate medical care. The authors call on the Georgian authorities to ensure that Burchuladze receives appropriate medical and legal assistance and is allowed regular contact with his family. The document also states that Burchuladze, who holds Georgian and Austrian citizenship, should be able to meet consular representatives without obstruction. The resolution’s authors reiterate their call for the EU to impose targeted sanctions and visa bans on individuals responsible for serious human rights violations. The document names Bidzina Ivanishvili, Irakli Kobakhidze, Shalva Papuashvili and Kakha Kaladze. The call also extends to other senior officials, as well as judges, prosecutors and law enforcement officers. The authors say Burchuladze’s case should be viewed in the context of democratic backsliding in Georgia, the weakening of judicial independence and Russia’s growing influence. They argue that Georgian Dream is using the judiciary and other state institutions to suppress dissent. The resolution’s authors call on the Georgian authorities to end the politically motivated persecution of artists, opposition figures, journalists and activists. They also demand independent investigations into reports of excessive force against protesters, intimidation and ill-treatment. The document stresses that progress toward EU membership requires respect for the rule of law, the European Convention on Human Rights, and fundamental rights. The accident occurred at 4:16 p.m. local time (1516 GMT) when a utility vehicle collided with a passenger car on National Road No. 1 towards In Amguel municipality, the authority said in a statement. The injured were evacuated to a local hospital for treatment, the statement read, adding that the toll was provisional and rescue operations were underway. Tamanrasset had seen a deadly crash a week earlier, which killed eight people. Road accidents in the North African country are mainly attributed to human factors, particularly traffic law violations, as well as poor road conditions, vehicle defects and adverse weather, according to official reports.

Joint military exercises between Belarus and Russia were held in the Brest and Gomel regions. These were scheduled exercises in 2022. Lukashenko noted that the US had warned that war might begin and informed Ukraine about troop concentrations near the borders, adding that he did not believe such a thing could happen. The Russians began withdrawing their troops by rail and road. The troops from Brest were withdrawn, but those remaining in other areas somehow turned toward Kyiv and decided to advance through it. You may ask why I didn't intervene and stop the Russians. But why should I have stopped them and fought for Ukraine? Ukraine was already at war with Belarus, Lukashenko said. In particular, he recalled the imposition of sanctions against Minsk, the closure of airspace, and the seizure of wagons. So why should I have defended Ukraine when the war started? Everyone knows we have no connection to this war. We do not want war; we do not need it, the self-proclaimed president summarized. The Limits of Illiberal Power: What the Defeats of Vucic and Orban Reveal
articles.summary: The similarities are striking, but so are the differences
articles.body: Within just a few months, two of Europe’s most entrenched political leaders, Viktor Orban in Hungary and Aleksandar Vucic in Serbia, lost power after more than a decade of increasingly authoritarian rule. In both countries, new opposition movements succeeded where their predecessors had failed for years, mobilising voters beyond traditional urban opposition strongholds and into smaller towns and rural areas long dominated by the governing parties. The similarities are striking, but so are the differences. Hungary’s opposition was led by Peter Magyar, a former government insider who built a highly centralised party, Tisza. Serbia’s emerged from a decentralised student protest movement that eventually formed an electoral alternative, the Student List. While both governments systematically captured state resources, political intimidation and violence was considerably more prominent under Vucic than under Orban. Yet both movements united voters across ideological divides and defeated seemingly unbeatable governments. Why did they succeed where their predecessors had failed? Economic difficulties, political scandals, government fatigue and changes in the media environment all contributed. But the comparison suggests that the most important transformation took place on the other side of politics – the opposition itself. There is some evidence that Hungarian and Serbian societies have become more liberal, particularly among younger voters. Yet research suggests that neither victory reflected a fundamental ideological transformation. In Hungary , liberal identification increased without fundamentally reshaping the country’s ideological landscape. Similarly, Serbia’s student movement attracted both pro-European and nationalist opposition voters, despite their persistent ideological differences. Both movements deliberately avoided presenting themselves as ideological alternatives to every aspect of the governments that they challenged. Magyar’s Tisza embraced national symbols and adopted Fidesz’s position on immigration, appealing to former government supporters as well as traditional opposition voters. Serbia’s students similarly avoided divisive questions such as Kosovo. Neither made progressive social policies or liberal values central to their campaigns. Instead, both united voters around a simpler promise: removing the existing government. Their success suggests that defeating an illiberal government does not necessarily require rejecting all the values it represents. Indeed, embracing some of those values may be essential to winning over its former supporters. For years, Hungary and Serbia were characterised by fragmented and discredited opposition parties that struggled to challenge the governments beyond major cities. Successive elections saw them compete for a limited electorate, while failing to convince voters that they offered a credible alternative to the governing parties. Tisza and the Student List broke with this pattern. Neither carried the political baggage of repeated electoral defeats or years of participation in a political system that many voters had come to distrust. They could therefore present themselves as a clear break with the existing order. Both movements also understood that their supporters were primarily dissatisfied with the political system itself, rather than with particular government policies. Their campaigns focused less on ideological disputes and more on defeating the incumbents and putting their countries ‘back on the right track’. Mass demonstrations, marches and direct challenges to the governments’ legitimacy became central to their political identity. Although earlier opposition parties had also protested corruption, their continued participation in the political system made it harder for them to represent a genuine break with it. Tisza and the Student List instead presented the elections as a choice between preserving the existing order and bringing it to an end. Perhaps most importantly, they gave voters a reason to believe that victory was actually possible. There was also something distinctly populist about their approach: they appealed to widespread frustration with the ruling political elite rather than offering a clearly defined alternative ideology. Yet the two movements differed considerably in their organisation. Tisza developed into a highly centralised, professionalised party centred around Magyar’s leadership, while Serbia’s Student List emerged from a decentralised movement based on grassroots decision-making. Their shared success therefore cannot be attributed to one particular organisational model. What mattered more was their novelty, their ability to mobilise beyond established opposition circles, and their determination to win. While the opposition’s transformation was crucial, the governments they faced had also become considerably more vulnerable. By 2026, Orban’s Fidesz had ruled Hungary for 16 years and Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) for 14. Over time, grievances, scandals and dissatisfaction accumulated, even among former government supporters. Long incumbency also became a liability: after more than a decade, it became increasingly difficult to blame previous governments or outside forces for economic problems, deteriorating public services or corruption. Economic conditions compounded these pressures. In Hungary, years of growth gave way to stagnation and high inflation, which reached 17.6 per cent in 2023, the highest in the EU. Even as inflation declined, households continued to face substantially higher prices, while withheld EU funds further restricted the government’s economic room for manoeuvre. Serbian households also experienced considerable inflation, although to a lesser degree. Yet economic dissatisfaction alone cannot explain the governments’ defeats. Both had survived previous elections despite mounting economic difficulties and public frustration. These conditions made the incumbents vulnerable, but why did they lose this time, rather than in earlier electoral cycles? Both governments spent years building up their influence over traditional media, particularly television, which remained an important source of political information for older and less politically engaged voters. But as online news and social media became increasingly influential, new opportunities emerged to communicate outside government-controlled channels. In Hungary, Fidesz invested heavily in online political advertising , particularly on Facebook and YouTube. However, Meta and Google stopped political advertising in the EU in 2025, restricting Fidesz’s campaigning ahead of the 2026 election. Meanwhile, Magyar built a highly successful organic social media presence. Serbia was different: outside the EU, Vucic’s party retained its online advertising advantage, but the students similarly used social media to communicate and organise independently. Neither movement relied on online campaigning alone. Both complemented their digital presence with extensive nationwide campaigns , visiting smaller towns and rural communities long dominated by the governing parties. By combining online communication with direct, face-to-face mobilisation, they reached voters who might otherwise have encountered little information beyond government-friendly media. Both opposition movements emerged from scandals that exposed the governments’ vulnerabilities. In Serbia, the collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad on November 1, 2024 killed 16 people and became a symbol of corruption and institutional failure. It triggered the student-led protests that eventually developed into a nationwide challenge to Vucic. In Hungary, the 2024 presidential pardon scandal revealed that the Fidesz-backed president had pardoned a children’s home official who helped cover up sexual abuse. The revelation undermined the government’s emphasis on child protection, forced the resignations of the president and Fidesz’s lead European Parliament candidate, and opened the way for Magyar’s political emergence. Despite their differences, both scandals made longstanding criticisms of corruption and unaccountability concrete and personal. Their significance lay not simply in the outrage they generated, but in their political consequences. Both governments had survived years of scandals and protests. What made these events different was that they helped bring about a transformation of the opposition itself. Perhaps the strongest evidence for the importance of opposition renewal comes from elections in which the new challengers were absent. In a Hungarian by-election in January 2025, Fidesz still won 64 per cent against the traditional opposition despite growing dissatisfaction. Similarly, in Serbian local elections later that year, Vucic’s governing coalition won 67 per cent against a largely traditional opposition alliance, although the vote was marred by reported irregularities. The comparison is even more striking in Hungary’s parliamentary elections. Fidesz received more than 2.1 million domestic votes in both the 2014 and 2026 elections. Yet while in 2014 this secured a two-thirds parliamentary majority for Fidesz, in 2026 it was Tisza that won such a super-majority. The decisive difference was the new opposition’s ability to unite previously fragmented voters , mobilise new supporters and attract former government voters. Economic problems, scandals and government fatigue made both governments vulnerable, but dissatisfaction alone was insufficient. It was the emergence of credible new opposition movements that turned dissatisfaction into electoral defeat. None of this means that opposition renewal alone would have been sufficient. Economic difficulties, scandals and government fatigue created the conditions for change, and without these crises, the new opposition movements might never have emerged. But it was their ability to turn widespread dissatisfaction into a credible political alternative that ultimately made the difference. The experiences of Hungary and Serbia demonstrate that even governments with extensive control over the media, state resources and political institutions are not invincible, as long as elections remain at least partly competitive. Orban and Vucic did not lose simply because voters had grown tired of them. They lost because, for the first time in years, enough voters believed there was someone capable of replacing them. Dániel Róna is a political scientist and director of the 21 Research Center. Fábián Spasic is an analyst at the 21 Research Center. The 21 Research Center is an independent Budapest-based research institute, specialising in public opinion polling, social research and political analysis. articles.title: Serbian Media Owner, Key Ally of Outgoing Administration, Arrested
articles.summary: Vucic himself confirmed the arrest in parliament, adding: “He was arrested only because of his journalistic work
articles.body: Dragan J Vucicevic, owner of the populist Serbian TV station Informer and a staunch supporter of the now-ousted administration of Aleksandar Vucic, was arrested on Wednesday on suspicion of “causing panic and disorder” and obstruction of justice. He was detained on the orders of the Second Basic Public Prosecutor’s Office in Belgrade according to Nova.rs, which said he will be placed in police custody for up to 48 hours. Vucic himself confirmed the arrest in parliament, adding: “He was arrested only because of his journalistic work.” According to the media outlet N1, Vucicevic will be brought before a prosecutor for questioning on Thursday. MPs from the Student List, which won recent elections in Serbia. applauded after Vucic’s confirmation of the arrest. After that, MPs from Vucic’s now opposition Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, left the parliamentary session for the police station where Vucicevic was being held. According to N1, that included the MPs Ana Brnabic and Milos Vucevic and a former State Secretary at the Interior Ministry, Dijana Hrkalovic. Vucicevic has been in the public spotlight since the Council of Serbia’s Regulatory Authority for Electronic Media, REM, launched two investigations into Informer. On November 16, the REM imposed two broadcasting bans on Informer, lasting 15 and 10 days respectively, as well as a seven-day ban on advertising between 6 p.m. and 9 p.m. At the time of publication, BIRN had no further details about the circumstances of Vucicevic’s arrest. BIRN asked the Ministry of Interior and the Second Basic Public Prosecutor’s Office for details, but neither replied.

articles.title: Filipovic and Becirovic host a Reception for BiH Statehood Day
articles.body: The members of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Darijana Filipović and Denis Bećirović, said this evening in Sarajevo, at the ceremonial reception on the occasion of BiH Statehood Day, that they see the country’s future in the European Union and NATO. Filipović pointed out that the equality of people and nations is a prerequisite for a functional state, and Bećirović reminded the message of the ZAVNOBiH councilor about Bosnia and Herzegovina as a common and indivisible homeland. Filipović said that she saw the oath she took a few days ago in the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a personal promise. Speaking about who institutions give space to, she stated that she wanted young scientists, professors, musicians, artists and athletes to receive an invitation to tonight’s reception, because even by choosing people they point out as role models, the elected representatives are sending a message to new generations. “Institutions are bigger than us who temporarily sit in them. Institutions belong to the people of this country,” said Filipović. She said that not everyone experiences November 25 in Bosnia and Herzegovina the same way, and that respect for the state should be earned. Speaking about what statehood means in everyday life, she singled out a court that judges everyone fairly, a school where every child has an equal opportunity, and a hospital where a person does not need an acquaintance. “Equality is not an obstacle to a functional state; it is a prerequisite for one. For in Bosnia and Herzegovina, we need neither domination nor obstruction. We need agreement, we need responsibility, and we need institutions that function,” said Filipović. She urged that political disputes be resolved within institutions and that, while preserving one’s own memories, respect be shown toward the victims of others. She linked BiH’s European future to a fair judiciary, responsible governance, free media, and a fair market, as well as to a political culture in which compromise is not perceived as betrayal. Bećirović paid tribute to anti-fascists and recalled that the delegates of ZAVNOBiH restored the statehood and territorial unity of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He specifically highlighted the phrase “indivisible homeland” from the Second Session of ZAVNOBiH, asserting that Bosnia and Herzegovina is an indivisible state. He advocated for the values of ZAVNOBiH to be more prominently featured in educational curricula, and for them to be the subject of further research and discussion at academic gatherings. He believes a special place belongs to the ZAVNOBiH Declaration on the Rights of Citizens, which affirms freedom of religion and conscience, assembly, association, and the press. According to him, it shares common ground with the American Declaration of Independence through the ideas of equality, freedom, and the protection of the individual against the arbitrary exercise of power by the authorities. He called upon academics, professors, business leaders, and prominent figures from the fields of culture and sports to engage more frequently in public discourse, while warning of the impact of disinformation and sensationalism. Addressing the preservation of peace and stability, he emphasized that European and Euro-Atlantic integration require concrete decisions. “The commitment to full membership in the European Union and NATO must not be mere political rhetoric; rather, it requires concrete action to reform the state in line with these goals. This is a strategic choice aimed at preserving peace and building a more economically developed nation,” stated Bećirović, while extending his congratulations on Statehood Day to the people of Bosnia and Herzegovina and those around the world. The reception at the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina was attended by diplomatic representatives, officials from international organizations and religious communities, as well as figures from the economic, academic, and cultural spheres of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Fena writes.

Sri Lankan asylum seeker killed himself after being sent by UK to Eswatini
articles.summary: Kishanth Peramalya was part of a group that set sail from India hoping to reach Canada and claim asylum there
articles.body: The UK sent a Sri Lankan asylum seeker who had been convicted of sexual assault to Eswatini, a southern African country to which he had no connection and where he killed himself. Kishanth Peramalya was part of a group that set sail from India hoping to reach Canada and claim asylum there. The boat was rescued by the Royal Navy in October 2021 when it got into difficulty and brought to Diego Garcia in the remote British Indian Ocean Territory, which hosts a US-UK military base. In November 2024, the UK allowed 61 migrants to enter from Diego Garcia after a damning UN report about conditions in the camp. However, the then home secretary, Yvette Cooper, denied Peramalya entry to the UK due to his criminal convictions while he was on Diego Garcia for four counts of sexual assault, one count of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and one count of arson. Cooper’s decision was upheld by UK courts. Peramalya had been granted protection from being returned to Sri Lanka, having been tortured and sexually abused by Sri Lankan military personnel as a teenager. In late March, the Maldives said it would take him for 30 days, according to the BBC . He was then transferred to Eswatini, a country landlocked by South Africa and Mozambique and formerly known as Swaziland, where he killed himself on 13 September. A draft deal between the UK and Eswatini governments would have committed Downing Street to cover the costs of Peramalya’s resettlement there for three years, according to the BBC, which said the UK was also finalising arrangements for Peramalya to live in Eswatini permanently. The Guardian has not seen the draft deal. Thabile Mdluli, a spokesperson for Eswatini’s government, said: “The initial arrangement was temporary in nature and intended to safeguard Mr Peramalya’s safety while the government of the United Kingdom worked towards a long-term solution regarding his circumstances.” She said that no formal agreement was ever reached over Peramalya’s long-term residency status with the UK and declined to comment further on the specific arrangements of his stay in Eswatini or the circumstances around his death. Mdluli said: “Eswatini has not received any other similar request from the government of the United Kingdom. The government of the Kingdom of Eswatini remains committed to ensuring that any agreements entered into with external partners safeguard national interest as well as the safety and security of Emaswati [Swazi people].” A UK government spokesperson said: “Keeping the British public safe will always be our first priority, and we will continue to take the decisions necessary to protect the British people. That includes taking steps to ensure high harm foreign criminals cannot enter the UK. We continue to work with the Eswatini authorities in relation to this case.” Peramalya had post-traumatic stress disorder and attempted suicide multiple times on Diego Garcia, according to a UK high court judgment in February 2025. Peramalya’s family told the BBC he was initially housed alone in an isolated guesthouse in Eswatini. “My brother did not want to go there at all,” said his sister, speaking from India. “He couldn’t manage being there alone, he was very lonely.” She said he had called her four times a day and was initially having weekly psychiatric appointments, which were made daily when his mental health deteriorated, as well as having someone brought in to prepare his food. Peramalya’s relatives said they were not aware of his convictions for sexual offences or any plan to make his transfer to Eswatini permanent. Eswatini has accepted dozens of third-country deportees from the US since July 2025. In November 2025, its government confirmed it had received $5.1m in exchange for taking up to 160 migrants from the US.

articles.title: Pro-Palestine activist sought by US in extradition case: ‘I still have a right to my beliefs’
articles.body: James “Fergie” Chambers, the wealthy leftwing activist and donor controversially sought in extradition by the US, has told the Guardian that he is “not asking anyone to endorse my ideas or not think I’m a jerk – but I still have a right to my beliefs and should not be unjustly accused because of them”. Chambers’s case is the first known instance of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation apparently tied to an international money-laundering charge in the criminal complaint underpinning the extradition request and donations to organizations helping Palestinians in Gaza. The complaint also includes riot and conspiracy to riot charges stemming from 2023 protests against New England branches of Israeli weapons manufacturer Elbit. Chambers was speaking from his Madrid apartment in his first in-depth interview after a Spanish appeals court ordered his provisional release on bail on Friday . That release was due to issues with the legally required US translation of the extradition request’s core documents into Spanish, first reported by the Guardian. “Support for my case doesn’t imply support of me, or my ideas,” Chambers said. “It’s about my right to have those ideas – and not be falsely accused of things.” Chambers, whose case has gained attention across the world, had been detained since 10 July, when Spanish authorities arrested him in Ibiza. The order granting Chambers’s provisional release asserted that the translation issues cause “a diminishment, at least for the time being, in the solidity or foundation of the extradition request”. Spanish judges had previously denied bail three times. The wealthy heir to at least $250mn from his family’s business – Atlanta–based Cox Enterprises – was in the middle of his first visit without being separated by glass with his mother, Lauren Hamilton, when he was summoned to receive the “good news” on Friday, Chambers told the Guardian. Minutes later, he returned to tell his mother he was being released. “She freaked out crying. We went nuts for about five minutes. Then we got to contacting my lawyer and getting my kids on a plane to Spain.” On Monday, Chambers’s five-year-old son with actor and activist Stella Schnabel could be heard in the background. The tableau was in stark contrast to his months in prison. “I tried to build a cocoon to deal with the immense unknown, the immense fear,” he said of his time in Aranjuez prison. “I would pray a lot. The only idea I could hold onto was, my home is the truth. The truth of who loves you. The truth of my own innocence. And the truth of what is happening in Palestine and all the things connected to what is happening in Palestine – other wars, gas prices. No one can take that away from you.” Chambers has been supported by his mother throughout his case, and has reconnected with his father, James Cox Chambers – who owns an estimated 17% stake in Cox Enterprises but does not play an active role in the company – for the first time in five years. “Speaking with my parents has provided emotional stability – and intelligent, adult minds to help make decisions,” Chambers said. Although he has had political disagreements with his father, a donor to the Democratic party, Chambers said his father “sees this situation as totally unthinkable and out of step with anything resembling a just society”. He also invoked his grandfather, the ACLU civil rights lawyer James Cox Hamilton, who died in 2014. “He would’ve turned in his grave over this,” Chambers said. While locked up, Chambers, a US citizen, received hundreds of letters of support from friends, family and strangers, postmarked from Atlanta to Barcelona – including, he said, “from a guy who had been imprisoned under [Spanish dictator Francisco] Franco, who painted the ‘ key of return ’ [a symbol of homes lost in the 1948 Nakba] on the Palestinian flag”. Chambers’s views and donations to progressive and humanitarian projects have been extensively profiled in US media, including his controversial public comments on Israel and Gaza. A week after the 7 October Hamas attacks on Israel, he posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/It’s simply genocide/Like it has been.” His release followed a separate decision on Thursday by a three-judge panel at Spain’s high court tasked with deciding on the extradition to pause the proceedings in order to evaluate the impact of the alterations the US made to the original, machine-made translation of the extradition request into Spanish. The US admitted to making several of the changes, calling them “substantial [and] inadvertent”. These and dozens of other changes introduced prejudicial notions with specific legal implications that in turn wound up in the Spanish prosecutor’s report on the case, Aitor Martínez, a member of Chambers’s defense team, told the Guardian last week. It was also recently revealed that there is no indictment behind the complaint, meaning the federal government has not had a grand jury evaluate evidence against Chambers, and instead is seeking his extradition based on the affidavit of a single FBI agent, the core of the sealed criminal complaint. During his time in prison, Chambers also began the process of applying for political asylum in Spain. He cannot be extradited until the asylum case runs its course, and also cannot be extradited if he is granted asylum. His legal team has notified the government office evaluating his asylum petition of the altered translations. Chambers was arrested 10 July as he and Schnabel pulled into the driveway of a school they were visiting to see about enrolling their five-year-old, part of plans to move to Spain. They had been staying in Ireland, where Schnabel was working on a film. Although the arrest came as a surprise – “I was confused! Did I speed?” he thought – Chambers revealed to the Guardian that a car had been following him around Dublin only days before, and that someone had broken into their car parked outside their house at night, without taking anything of value. “I noticed signs of surveillance,” he said. Months later, last Wednesday, Irish police raided the same house, acting on a request from US authorities. With his immediate future uncertain, Chambers said he was “looking forward to sharing a couple of nice dinners with my family this week”. As for the past, he said the millions he has donated to an estimated 100 projects in about 20 countries is “the most important thing I’ve done”. “Somebody with the political orientation I have and with resources, no matter how good of an activist I am, it’s not gonna be as effective as medical aid or feeding children in Gaza, supporting independent media that wouldn’t otherwise exist, or paying people’s bail who have been arrested for protesting. “I’m giving a lot of money to things that other people aren’t giving money to.” Chambers also said he was “grateful for the way Spanish courts have dealt with this – just focusing on the facts. It shouldn’t matter that I’ve made some emotional statements.”

Second Uzbekistan–Azerbaijan interparliamentary forum opens in Baku
articles.summary: The forum brings together members of Uzbekistan's Oliy Majlis and Azerbaijan's Milli Majlis
articles.body: Tashkent, Uzbekistan (UzDaily.uz) — The second Uzbekistan–Azerbaijan interparliamentary forum has opened in Baku, focusing on strengthening the two countries' relations of enduring friendship and alliance, the press service of Uzbekistan's Senate of the Oliy Majlis reported. The forum brings together members of Uzbekistan's Oliy Majlis and Azerbaijan's Milli Majlis, as well as representatives of the two countries' youth parliaments. The opening session featured addresses by Tanzila Narbayeva, Chairperson of the Senate of Uzbekistan's Oliy Majlis, and Sahiba Gafarova, Speaker of Azerbaijan's Milli Majlis. Participants said that political will, personal friendship and mutual trust between the two countries' leaders had elevated Uzbekistan–Azerbaijan relations to the level of an alliance. Two years ago, the presidents signed a Treaty on Allied Relations. Another important milestone was the third meeting of the Supreme Interstate Council, held in Tashkent in August 2026. Following the meeting, the two presidents signed a Treaty on Eternal Friendship. Interparliamentary cooperation plays an important role in bilateral relations. The first forum of this format was held in Khiva in July 2025. The Khiva Declaration adopted at the meeting set priorities for parliamentary cooperation and reaffirmed the commitment to strengthening friendship, strategic partnership and alliance. Since then, the two sides have expanded political dialogue and signed dozens of documents covering key areas of bilateral cooperation. Joint projects, trade and economic ties, investment links and cooperation between regions have also developed. More than 470 enterprises with Azerbaijani capital operate in Uzbekistan. More than 130 companies with Uzbek investment operate in Azerbaijan. Given the role of parliaments in implementing interstate agreements and providing legislative support for reforms, participants proposed developing cooperation over the next two years in four areas. The first involves parliamentary oversight of the implementation of bilateral agreements. The second aims to increase regional participation in interparliamentary dialogue. The third focuses on strengthening cooperation at international parliamentary platforms. The fourth concerns direct links between educational, scientific and cultural institutions. The forum also highlighted the importance of youth exchange programmes and support for joint initiatives to preserve the shared historical and cultural heritage of the Uzbek and Azerbaijani peoples.

Teen’s homicidal thoughts dismissed as ‘crap’ days before she killed 10-year-old, inquest hears
articles.summary: Just 48 hours later, the teenager killed 10-year-old Bridgette “Biddy” Porter at a property in rural NSW
articles.body: Two days before a teenager killed a young girl while in the grips of psychosis, her father dismissed her homicidal thoughts, delusions and visions as “crap”, an inquest has been told. On 6 July 2020, the 14-year-old wrote in her diary: “I’m getting sick and tired of being told I’m a liar when I say I see cat eyes in a dark room and feel like I’m going to kill someone.” Just 48 hours later, the teenager killed 10-year-old Bridgette “Biddy” Porter at a property in rural NSW. Biddy, remembered as a clever, creative and kind child, died of multiple injuries while staying at the farm in the school holidays on 8 July 2020. During closing submissions at an inquest on Thursday, the barrister representing Biddy’s parents argued it was unreasonable for the teenager’s parents not to seek urgent help. “It is open to this court to make findings there were a constellation of symptoms they were aware of,” Tahn O’Rourke told the NSW coroner’s court in Lidcombe on Thursday. “They were aware they were linked … and that there was a potentially serious mental illness emerging.” The teenager killed six chickens on the family farm in mid-2019 and subsequently told relatives about hearing voices, experiencing visions and having a sense of not feeling real, the inquest was told. In the weeks before attacking Biddy, the teenager told her mother she thought about killing people “all the time”, including her parents. The mother said she did not seek mental health support for the girl because it did not occur to her. “I never believed in mental health. I didn’t understand mental health, so it didn’t come up to me as something I needed to do,” she told the inquest in June. The father’s police statement said he told the teenager her visions and violent thoughts were “crap and she was just looking for attention”, O’Rourke said. The mother sought advice from a naturopath in mid-2020, who told her to go to a GP. The GP referred the family to a psychiatrist soon before the killing, but didn’t organise urgent care because the mother did not reveal the teenager’s violence or homicidal thoughts, the inquest was told. Biddy’s killer, who cannot be identified, was charged with murder, but a NSW supreme court judge ruled she was not criminally responsible due to mental illness in 2021. The teenager, who has been diagnosed with schizophrenia and was in acute psychosis at the time of the killing, remains in a forensic facility. Counsel assisting Dr Peggy Dwyer SC said the actions of the parents should be seen in the context of evidence that early symptoms of schizophrenia can be “vague” and hard to separate from typical teenage behaviour. Forensic psychiatrist Olav Nielssen gave evidence the girl’s early development of schizophrenia was “extremely rare” and he had never seen a presentation like hers before. “[They] were not aware [she] was suffering a serious mental health condition … even if looking back now, it seems so obvious,” Dwyer said. State coroner Teresa O’Sullivan will hand down findings and recommendations at a later date. In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact the Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800; adults can seek help at Blue Knot Foundation on 1300 657 380

articles.title: EU sets energy truce, Black Sea deal as terms for Russia talks — EC
articles.summary: PARIS, November 25
articles.body: PARIS, November 25. /TASS/. The European Commission wants Russia to halt attacks on energy infrastructure this winter and agree to a truce in the Black Sea as conditions for entering into negotiations on Ukraine and European security, said European Commission (EC) head Ursula von der Leyen. Von der Leyen told a European Parliament session in Strasbourg that the EU's demands include a "winter ceasefire on energy infrastructure and a truce to ensure the safe passage of food exports through the Black Sea." At a November 13 summit in Brussels, EU leaders again failed to appoint a negotiator on Ukraine or determine the EU's negotiating position. Instead, they confirmed that the EU could be represented at the technical negotiations by a group of seven people led by von der Leyen's chief of staff Bjoern Seibert, who traveled to Abu Dhabi as part of a support group for Ukraine. This group will include representatives of the EC and the European Council, four EU states - Germany, France, Italy and Poland - as well as the UK, which is not part of the EU.

articles.title: Israel trying to deceive U.S. into war with chemical weapons claim, Iran says
articles.body:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday that Israel was trying to drag the United States into another war after an Israeli minister alleged Tehran is building chemical weapons.

"This warmonger shamelessly accuses Iran ... of developing and concealing such heinous weapons in pharmaceutical factories. The objective is audacious: to deceive the US into fighting yet another war on its behalf," he wrote in a statement posted on X.

Israel has for years accused Iran of trying to acquire nuclear weapons, but Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz on Tuesday alleged Tehran is building chemical weapons and vowed to stop the Islamic republic from obtaining them.

"Iran is in the process of developing chemical weapons but has not yet reached the capability to attack Israel with them," said Katz in a statement published by his Likud party on Telegram. He also left open the possibility of preemptive strikes against Iran.

"We must not allow this to proceed," he said.

President Trump mentioned the same thing to Fox News earlier this month on his Asia trip, saying, "Well, there is indication that Iran is looking at gases, looking at bio, because we've shut them out with the nuclear. ... Nuclear is much harder, and they're looking at gas and they're looking at the bio, the biological weapons."

CBS/AFP

Iran developing chemical weapons, Israeli defense minister says, warns of possible preemptive strike
articles.summary: Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said on Tuesday that Iran is developing chemical weapons, and vowed to stop Tehran from obtaining them
articles.body:
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said on Tuesday that Iran is developing chemical weapons, and vowed to stop Tehran from obtaining them.

"Iran is in the process of developing chemical weapons," Katz said in a briefing to Israeli reporters, according to public broadcaster KAN and other national outlets. "The state of Israel will not allow them to reach that capability."

In his briefing on Tuesday, Katz floated the possibility of a preemptive strike against Tehran, if necessary.

"If we recognize that the Iranians intend to attack Israel, can't we tell the army to attack earlier and thwart the threat?" he said, according to a transcript from Israel's Channel 12. "If the Iranians attack us first, it will be a failure."

Katz's comments came at the same time as Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi criticized the U.S. government for not funding the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons, the international body that monitors and combats chemical weapons use at The Hague. The organization is facing a budget crisis because the U.S. has pulled funding, according to a Reuters report.

"The U.S. is so concerned about chemical arms that it's crippling the world's chemical weapons watchdog," Araghchi wrote Tuesday on X. "OPCW may be forced to suspend work and scale back vital programs. By obstructing its mandate, the U.S. is deliberately putting global peace and security at risk. Shameful."

The OPCW won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2013 for its work in Syria.

CBS/AFP

North Korea's Kim urges wider tactical nuclear weapons deployment on facility tour, KCNA says
articles.summary: KCNA did not identify the facilities or their locations
articles.body: North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, left, inspects work on nuclear material production and nuclear weapons research, Wednesday, in this photo released by the Korean Central News Agency the next day. Yonhap North Korean leader Kim Jong-un said his country should focus on deploying tactical nuclear weapons across multiple domains and that its nuclear material production capacity was being systematically expanded, state media KCNA reported on Thursday. Kim, who spoke during an inspection on Wednesday of nuclear material production and weapons research facilities, also said North Korea's status as a nuclear weapons state was "absolutely inviolable." KCNA did not identify the facilities or their locations. "Our nuclear capability is now a reality," KCNA quoted Kim as saying. Kim said North Korea should "focus on utilizing tactical nuclear weapons across multiple domains for different missions" and called recent achievements in nuclear weapons production a major success for the country's nuclear force policy. The tour of the nuclear facilities appears aimed at underscoring Pyongyang's push to expand and diversify its nuclear arsenal in defiance of calls for denuclearization, as questions persist over prospects for renewed dialogue with the United States. Tactical nuclear weapons are generally lower-yield warheads meant for battlefield use, unlike strategic weapons designed for longer-range strikes. In 2023, KCNA published images of what it called the Hwasan-31 tactical nuclear warhead, saying it could be fitted to a range of delivery systems, including short-range missiles. Photographs released by KCNA on Thursday showed Kim and officials inspecting objects that analysts said looked like gas centrifuges, used to enrich uranium, and miniaturized, standardized tactical nuclear warheads such as the Hwasan-31. Kim also said any attempt to deny North Korea's nuclear status, which it enshrined in its constitution in 2023, would be regarded as "an open declaration of war." "Our possession of nuclear weapons is an absolutely irreversible choice as long as malicious forces exist that use nuclear weapons as a means of achieving hegemony," Kim said. Kim cites US nuclear alliances Kim justified the buildup by citing what he described as growing nuclear threats from the United States and its allies. The United States had "incited its vassal states" near North Korea to acquire nuclear-powered submarines by introducing the "dangerous precedent of nuclear proliferation through AUKUS to Northeast Asia," he said, referring to the trilateral security pact involving the United States, Britain and Australia. He also accused Washington of building a "nuclear military alliance system" by trying to share and use nuclear weapons with its allies. South Korea is pursuing nuclear-powered submarines after U.S. President Donald Trump approved the plan in October last year. The topic has also been under discussion in Japan. Analysts said the visit carried a message for Washington amid speculation about U.S.-North Korea diplomatic contact. "This is not so much North Korea permanently closing the door to dialogue with the United States as a strategy of raising the bar: 'denuclearisation talks' are over, and if talks open in future, it will deal only on a 'nuclear state versus nuclear state' basis," said Lim Eul-chul, a professor at South Korea's Kyungnam University. Shin Jong-woo, secretary-general of the Korea Defence and Security Forum, said Kim's reference to "multiple domains" could signal targets beyond the Korean peninsula, including the U.S. mainland. Kim's intent "seems to be that with no alternatives now, Pyongyang will build up its nuclear forces further and head toward a setup in which it can confront the U.S.," Shin said. North Korea has conducted six nuclear tests since 2006, with its last and most powerful test in 2017. South Korea's defence minister said in August that Pyongyang was believed to possess between 80 and 120 nuclear warheads, but said the estimate came from private research organisations and could not be officially confirmed.

articles.title: Palestinian journalist killed by Israel in Gaza wins Rory Peck prize
articles.summary: Dagga, who has a teenage son named Ghaith, was killed in August 2025 in an Israeli airstrike on a southern Gaza hospital
articles.body: Mariam Dagga, the Palestinian war correspondent who was killed at the age of 33 in Gaza in an Israeli strike, has posthumously won the prestigious Rory Peck prize for freelance video journalists, the organisers announced on Wednesday. She shares the award with two of her colleagues from the Associated Press (AP), Abdel Kareem Hana and Jehad Alshrafi, “for their powerful coverage of the human cost of the war” in the Palestinian territory, the Rory Peck Trust said. Dagga, who has a teenage son named Ghaith, was killed in August 2025 in an Israeli airstrike on a southern Gaza hospital , which claimed the lives of four other journalists. The independent photographer and reporter had been working with the AP news agency since the beginning of the current conflict, triggered by Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attack on Israel. Dagga was renowned for her relentless reporting despite the personal losses she suffered throughout the war. She filmed the death of a protester who was shot during the 2018 Great March of Return in Gaza , when Israeli forces shot protesters marching towards the Gaza border fence, killing more than 220 people and wounding more than 9,200. She later discovered that the protester was her brother. The war correspondent continued her work as a journalist during the war in Gaza over the last 22 months, working as a freelancer with the AP and Independent Arabia. The AP’s executive editor, Julie Pace, said: “Journalists play an essential role in documenting events and informing the public, often at enormous personal risk. “We honour Mariam and all journalists killed during this conflict and other conflicts – and remain committed to seeking answers about their deaths.” French photographer Robin Tutenges was the recipient of the first Rory Peck award for photojournalism in recognition of his work on the conflict in Ethiopia’s northern Amhara region. Sudanese freelance photographer and video journalist Ahmed Mohamed Abdalla, who works with Agence France-Presse, was shortlisted for the same award for his coverage of the fall of El Fasher to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces in Sudan’s civil war. Abdalla was not allowed to attend the prize-giving ceremony in London as the UK government refused to grant him a visa. In a recorded video message shared during the ceremony, he told of how the capital of the North Darfur region’s besieged inhabitants had to eat livestock feed to survive amid the daily deluge of missiles. The prize has been awarded since 1995 in memory of Northern Irish video journalist Rory Peck, who was killed in Moscow in 1993, to celebrate the work of freelance video journalists.

articles.title: AfD co-leader says no peace in Europe without working with US, Russia
articles.summary: BERLIN, November 25
articles.body: BERLIN, November 25. /TASS/. Peace in Europe can only be reached together with Russia and the United States, and the coalition of the willing on Ukraine only hinders efforts to resolve the conflict, Alice Weidel, a co-chairwoman of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) opposition party, argued. "Your 'coalition of the willing' is actually a coalition of the helpless," the politician said during debates on the 2027 draft budget at the Bundestag, addressing German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. "It does not contribute to putting an end to the Ukraine conflict, but stands in the way of peace. Remember one thing: peace in Europe is only possible jointly with Russia and the United States, not without them," she stressed. Weidel pointed out that Germany spends €18 billion annually on Ukraine, including the costs of accommodating refugees from this country in Germany and €11.5 billion as military aid to Kiev. Alongside her AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla, Weidel called Ukraine "one of the most corrupt countries," noting that Germany will soon be the only nation to finance Kiev. "For your personal vanity, Mr. Merz, you are leading Germany to a geopolitical sideline, destroying our image in the international arena and putting our country on the verge of state bankruptcy. The outcome of your rule and the rule of this government will be a catastrophe," Weidel concluded. Germany is Ukraine’s largest donor. Since the start of the special military operation on February 24, 2022, Berlin has provided Kiev with around €45.7 billion worth of humanitarian and €57.8 billion worth of military aid. Apart from official channels, various private and public German organizations regularly send humanitarian aid to Ukraine. Meanwhile, the Russian side has repeatedly stated that weapons supplies to the Kiev regime only protract the Ukraine conflict.

articles.title: Poland to introduce no-fly zone in east amid Russian missile threat
articles.body: The Polish government is preparing a regulation that will ban flights a dozen to several dozen kilometres from Poland's eastern border following incidents that involved Russian missiles violating Polish airspace, a deputy defence minister has said. Cezary Tomczyk said on Wednesday that the government wanted a relevant regulation to come into force at the end of December 2026 or in early January 2027. He said the no-fly zone is necessary to facilitate the already introduced "positive identification", a procedure under which a military pilot, "based on information from radars, allies, altitude and speed" will be able to "identify and then, if necessary, engage" an aerial object. In the early hours on Friday, three Russian cruise missiles violated Polish airspace and crashed in various locations in eastern and southeastern Poland. On Tuesday morning a likely Russian reconnaissance drone briefly entered Polish airspace. (PAP)

articles.title: Kremlin brushes off reports of up to 700,000 Russian war deaths
articles.body:
The Kremlin also declined to comment on reports that up to 700,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in its almost five-year-long offensive on Ukraine.

After analysing a trove of hacked data from Russia’s official statistics agency, several Russian and international media outlets say Moscow’s own data shows 470,000-700,000 soldiers have been killed in the war.

Russia has not given an official death toll among its army since September 2022, when it said almost 6,000 soldiers had been killed in the first six months of fighting – a figure widely seen as a large undercount even at the time.

Asked about the new reports, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Wednesday:

“The only entity that can officially disclose casualty figures is the defence ministry of the Russian Federation.”

“I suggest not to pay attention to any other data,” he added.

editorialRejections.body: Moldovan president says Russia does not want to end war President Maia Sandu believes that drones entering the country’s airspace represent both a consequence of the intensification of Russian attacks on Ukraine and the result of deliberate actions aimed at testing the authorities’ response and intimidating the population. The head of state said that, in her opinion, Russia currently does not want to end the war in Ukraine and that pressure on Moscow must increase, in order to improve the chances of peace. She made statements to this effect today evening at the Secrets of Power programme, broadcast on Jurnal TV, in the context of recent incidents in which more drones entered the airspace of Moldova. Referring to the recorded cases, including the one of a drone that flew over Chisinau from north to south and reached the area of the international airport, Maia Sandu said there had been more explanations for these incidents. “I believe it is a combination. Of course, the increase in the number of cases is determined by the increase in the number of attacks on Ukraine, because we see what a terrible situation is unfolding there, and when the regions bordering Moldova are targeted, drones also reach us. But it is clear that, in some cases, there are also deliberate actions, or actions that test our response and seek to intimidate us. It is not only Moldova’s case. You saw what happened in Poland a few days ago,” the head of state said. According to Maia Sandu, the intensification of Russian attacks on Ukraine and actions affecting other countries as well increase the risks for the citizens of Moldova. “This is a more advanced level of aggression on the part of the Russian Federation, primarily toward Ukraine, in terms of what it is doing to cities and villages and to civilians, but also toward other states. Obviously, the greater the number, the greater the risk for our citizens,” the president said. In the same context, Maia Sandu referred to what she described as a paradox between diplomatic efforts to stop the war and the intensification of military actions. “We are somehow living through a paradox on this period. There is a great deal of discussion about peace. Some meetings are taking place in neutral locations. We hear all sorts of promises that peace is just around the corner. At the same time, however, the war is growing in scale. There are powerful strikes that carry great weight, both literally and figuratively, from both sides,” the head of state said. Asked whether international efforts could lead to a ceasefire and the restoration of peace, the president said that, in her opinion, Russia is not interested in stopping the war. “It is true that efforts are being made to reach a ceasefire and restore peace. The problem is that Russia does not want this. That is my opinion. Based on what I have seen and heard, I do not believe that Putin wants to stop this war. If he wanted to, they are the ones who could stop it, and there would be no more war,” Maia Sandu said. The head of state noted that American and European partners were making diplomatic efforts, but she believes these will not produce results, as long as Moscow does not want to end the war. “The partners, both the Americans and the Europeans, are of course trying and holding discussions. I do not believe that these actions will lead to results, because Russia, under Putin’s regime, does not want to stop the war. I believe it will exploit this winter,” the president said. In her opinion, increasing pressure on Moscow, including through sanctions and measures affecting the Russian economy, is necessary to improve the chances of peace. “To enhance the chances of peace, pressure on Moscow must be increased. This means sanctions; Russia’s economy must be weakened, because as long as the economy can generate resources, they will be directed toward producing even more military equipment, more ballistic missiles, drones and so on, which are used to kill people in Ukraine,” Maia Sandu said. The president also said that, in her opinion, the Russian authorities were trying to create the impression that they are interested in peace negotiations, while continuing their attacks on Ukraine. “I do not believe that the regime in Moscow is genuinely interested in these peace talks at this time. I believe they are only trying to create the impression that they are interested in these discussions, but in reality, they will continue doing what they have done until now: brutally attacking Ukraine,” the head of state concluded. editorialRejections.title: Trump, NATO chief urge Russia not to ‘expand’ Ukraine war
editorialRejections.reason: US coverage requires an international or US news source
editorialRejections.body: West Palm Beach: US President Donald Trump and NATO chief Mark Rutte urged Russia not to “expand the war” in Ukraine, in a joint statement issued Wednesday after meeting in Florida. The “outstanding” and “very impactful” meeting focused on the wars in Ukraine and Iran, said the statement issued by the White House after the closed-door talks at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago resort. “We also discussed the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war, and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the war as rapidly as possible,” the statement added. The joint appeal by Trump and Rutte comes despite the US leader describing Russian President Vladimir Putin as “my friend” during a meeting in China last week. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has taken issue with Trump’s comments on Putin. Rutte was asked about Trump’s comments in an interview with Fox News’ “Fox & Friends” on Wednesday. “What President Trump is doing, also in the meeting in Shenzhen, is testing Putin,” the NATO secretary general said. “How serious is he? Is he willing to come to the negotiating table? Is he willing to really engage in talks. “So let’s keep the pressure on. I think it is working, and we have to keep that going.” Trump, accused by critics of siding with Moscow over Kyiv, said following his meeting with Putin that the Russian leader wants to see the war end by “diplomatic means.” The Florida meeting comes as European nations have expressed a desire to join preliminary talks that have so far only included Ukraine, the United States and Russia. Rutte said any agreement is going to have to include security guarantees for Ukraine. “When the war ends, either with a peace deal, preferable, or if not possible, a long-term ceasefire, we need to make sure that Ukraine has the security guarantees going forward,” he said. “But the most important thing here,” Rutte added, “is that we have to make sure that Ukraine has what it needs to keep the fight going, being so successful and putting that maximum pressure on the Russians.” Trump and Rutte also discussed increasing defense spending, which the US president has pressed European powers to do, the joint statement said. The Florida talks also came as Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth is expected to announce in coming weeks a review of the US force presence in Europe.
